# Lesson evidence in one line each

49 lessons. This is the one file that lists every lesson (besides llms-full.txt, which holds everything). To choose lessons: scan this file, then open the aspect page (the heading link) only for the lessons you use; it holds the full "Against" line, the Era (years and newest model family) and the legend. Each line: ID, tag (stated by a source, or ours), the lesson, then model (does it depend on model ability), people (what checked its evidence: people, people in part, a checker, a model, or none but the author), strength, "may be outdated" where it applies, the cases it cites ("(own)" marks the maintainer's own project, never counted toward strength), and the cases its "Against" line cites.

## [Build loops](build-loops.md)

- **BLD-1** [stated] A single agent's interface build can look finished while its core feature fails; a second agent that used the running app and tested agreed criteria caught specific bugs, and the core feature worked. Model yes; people none; weak. Cases: Anthropic harness. Against: none found.
- **BLD-2** [stated] For an agent that reviews and fixes code, a read-only reviewer and a separate fixer that pass fixed templates through a parent worked better than many parallel specialists. Model partly; people none; weak. Cases: GitHub a11y agent. Against: none found.
- **BLD-3** [stated] Tell a repair loop which violations remain: one told only of parse or structure failures cost more and fixed no more; one fed a model-written violation report beat the plain prompt on average. Model partly; people checker; medium. Cases: Concordia repair, UCI code study. Against: none found.
- **BLD-4** [stated] An agent told to stop and hand work to people may look for ways to write code anyway; back the stop rule with explicit instructions against working around it. Model yes; people none; weak. Cases: GitHub a11y agent. Against: none found.
- **BLD-5** [stated] Grading criteria written into a builder's prompt steer its designs before any feedback, and one phrase in them can pull designs toward the same look. Model yes; people none; weak. Cases: Anthropic harness. Against: none found.
- **BLD-6** [stated] A planner, builder and grader harness cost many times a solo run, though the grader's own share was small; the grader paid off only on work beyond what the model built reliably alone. Model partly; people none; weak. Cases: Anthropic harness. Against: none found.
- **BLD-7** [stated] When the model changes, remove harness parts one at a time and keep those that still change the result; cutting many at once hid which parts mattered. Model partly; people none; weak. Cases: Anthropic harness. Against: none found.
- **BLD-8** [ours] After a grading agent passes a build, walk each whole job as a newcomer; a build that passed its per-feature tests kept a workflow the screen never explained. Model partly; people none; weak. Cases: Anthropic harness. Against: none found.
- **BLD-9** [stated] When parallel lanes rebuild an interface, keep each old page answering inside the new frame until its replacement lands, so the product keeps working after each merge. Model no; people checker; weak. Cases: studio-go (own). Against: none found.
- **BLD-10** [stated] Lanes that own a fixed list of files stop to ask for one-line edits in shared lists and tests; let them make and name such edits, and turn shared lists into registrations. Model partly; people none; weak. Cases: studio-go (own). Against: none found.

## [Accessibility](accessibility.md)

- **ACC-1** [stated] Code models writing pages without being asked for accessibility handle basic rules such as contrast and alt text better than the human code they replaced, and do worse on ARIA. Model yes; people checker; medium; may be outdated. Cases: UCI code study. Against: none found.
- **ACC-2** [stated] Asking a model for accessible code, with rules, examples or a self-review, almost never beat the plain prompt; the broad instructions added attributes that broke other rules. Model yes; people checker; medium; may be outdated. Cases: UCI code study. Against: none found.
- **ACC-3** [stated] Model-written accessibility fixes lowered the checker's count on most pages but left only about a quarter of pages clean; count what remains after each fix, not only what went away. Model yes; people checker; medium. Cases: Concordia repair. Against: none found.
- **ACC-4** [stated] A model's fix that is right for one element can break the rest of the page (duplicate IDs, ARIA that hides focusable content, misused roles); re-check the whole page after each fix. Model yes; people checker; medium. Cases: Concordia repair, UCI code study. Against: none found.
- **ACC-5** [stated] A falling checker rate, or code that passes the checks, is no proof a page works for disabled users: such rates count all violations alike, and checkers miss ARIA meaning and keyboard use. Model no; people partly; medium. Cases: UCI code study, GitHub a11y agent, Agentic audit. Against: none found.
- **ACC-6** [stated] As a detector, a model matched a rule checker on whole pages and agreed with it most on roles and labels, but flagged far more markup problems and diverged on layout. Model yes; people checker; medium. Cases: Concordia repair. Against: none found; a limit from Agentic audit.
- **ACC-7** [stated] An agent per WCAG criterion that operates the page found more of the failures expert audits reported than axe-core or a single-pass model, and raised more findings the audits never listed. Model yes; people yes; medium. Cases: Agentic audit. Against: none found; a limit from Concordia repair, Agentic audit.
- **ACC-8** [stated] Per-criterion browser agents matched both reported keyboard traps and nearly all keyboard failures; every batch model reading a screenshot and the accessibility tree missed both traps. Model yes; people yes; weak. Cases: Agentic audit. Against: none found; a limit from Agentic audit.
- **ACC-9** [stated] Listing the criteria in a coding agent's audit request raised both the reported failures it found and its findings the audits never listed; measure both when changing the request. Model yes; people yes; weak. Cases: Agentic audit. Against: none found.
- **ACC-10** [stated] Score a checker that may decline against every known failure and keep what it declines as open work; recall on the items it answered hides the failures it skipped. Model partly; people yes; medium. Cases: Agentic audit. Against: none found.
- **ACC-11** [stated] An audit report's silence is a weak pass: score a checker's findings on unlisted items against it, but keep them as candidates for a person to settle and never fold them into the labels. Model no; people partly; medium. Cases: Agentic audit. Against: none found.
- **ACC-12** [ours] Before scoring a detector, confirm with the same checker that the pages labelled clean are clean; otherwise its precision partly measures the labels, not the detector. Model no; people checker; medium. Cases: Concordia repair. Against: none found.
- **ACC-13** [ours] Before quoting or comparing an accessibility agent's fix rate, find out what counts as fixed, out of what total, and who decided; a seller's headline rate may define none of them. Model no; people none; weak. Cases: GitHub a11y agent. Against: none found.
- **ACC-14** [stated] Give an accessibility agent your own archive of logged issues and the changes that fixed them; the author holds generic best-practice prompts fall short, as models lean toward inaccessible code. Model partly; people none; weak. Cases: GitHub a11y agent, UCI code study. Against: none found.
- **ACC-15** [stated] Keep an accessibility agent off complex code and off widgets experts mark high-risk, such as drag and drop or data grids, and send them to people. Model partly; people none; weak. Cases: GitHub a11y agent. Against: none found.

## [Model judges](model-judges.md)

- **JDG-1** [stated] Before using a model as a rater of interfaces, compare its ratings with people's on the same items, and choose the judge and its inputs by that agreement. Model partly; people yes; medium. Cases: ArtifactsBench, UW walkthrough, UW heuristic review, Brazil heuristic review. Against: none found.
- **JDG-2** [stated] A judge of generated pages agreed with experts more often when it saw screenshots of the rendered page and the code together than with either alone. Model yes; people yes; medium; may be outdated. Cases: ArtifactsBench. Against: none found.
- **JDG-3** [ours] Quote a judge's agreement with people only from items it was not tuned on, with the size of that set, and measure it again whenever the judge model changes. Model partly; people yes; medium. Cases: ArtifactsBench, UW heuristic review. Against: none found.
- **JDG-4** [ours] When a judge ranks models that include its own maker's, check the top ranks with a judge from another maker before trusting the order. Model partly; people model; weak. Cases: ArtifactsBench. Against: none found.
- **JDG-5** [stated] A model grading its own interface work rates it too kindly; a separate grading agent is easier to make sceptical, though it starts out inclined to be lenient toward model output. Model yes; people none; weak. Cases: Anthropic harness. Against: none found; a limit from UW heuristic review.
- **JDG-6** [stated] An untuned model acting as QA found real bugs, then argued them away and approved the build; tune it on logs where its verdict differs from a person's. Model yes; people none; weak. Cases: Anthropic harness. Against: none found.
- **JDG-7** [stated] Reviewing app screenshots against usability heuristics, one model covered more of the known issues than a single expert or a pool of five experts. Model yes; people yes; medium; may be outdated. Cases: UW heuristic review. Against: disagree: Brazil heuristic review.
- **JDG-8** [stated] Reviewing still screens, a model found fewer of the experts' problems on user control in both studies, and in one study few on efficiency and memory load; keep people on those. Model yes; people yes; medium; may be outdated. Cases: Brazil heuristic review, UW heuristic review. Against: disagree: UW heuristic review.
- **JDG-9** [stated] A model reviewing screenshots raises non-issues (problems not on the screen, misread status icons or banners, common conventions taken as faults); have a person confirm each finding. Model yes; people yes; strong; may be outdated. Cases: UW heuristic review, Brazil heuristic review. Against: none found.
- **JDG-10** [stated] A model reviewing a sequence of screenshots repeats an issue on every screen where it recurs and misses about half the problems that span screens, even when told to weigh the flow. Model yes; people yes; medium; may be outdated. Cases: UW heuristic review, Brazil heuristic review. Against: none found.
- **JDG-11** [stated] A model's heuristic review adds issues experts did not list, with more on wording and visual design than the experts found; use it beside experts, not in place of them. Model yes; people yes; medium; may be outdated. Cases: Brazil heuristic review, UW heuristic review. Against: none found.
- **JDG-12** [stated] Across a review of several tasks a model reviewer kept its coverage from task to task while experts found less as they went, and repeat runs returned most of its first list. Model yes; people partly; medium; may be outdated. Cases: UW heuristic review. Against: none found.
- **JDG-13** [ours] Before quoting a model reviewer's overlap with an expert list, merge its repeats across screens and mark which expert issues could be seen in what the model was shown. Model partly; people yes; medium. Cases: Brazil heuristic review. Against: none found.

## [Simulated users](simulated-users.md)

- **SIM-1** [stated] A model that walks tasks in a person's place finishes more of them, in fewer steps and on straighter paths, so its run is no estimate of what the tasks cost people. Model yes; people yes; medium. Cases: UW walkthrough. Against: none found; a limit from studio-go (own).
- **SIM-2** [stated] Asked like people to say what confuses it, a simulated user voices far fewer doubts; an explicit confusion rating per screen during the walk recovers where people hesitate. Model yes; people yes; medium. Cases: UW walkthrough. Against: none found.
- **SIM-3** [stated] Give a simulated user the history of its walk when it rates screens; the same screens rated one at a time gave weak ratings that changed from run to run. Model partly; people yes; medium. Cases: UW walkthrough. Against: none found.
- **SIM-4** [ours] Run a simulated user several times and measure how far the runs agree before acting on one run's ratings. Model partly; people partly; medium. Cases: UW walkthrough. Against: none found.

## [Measuring jobs](measuring-jobs.md)

- **JOB-1** [stated] Tests that every page follows the interface rules can all pass while the user's jobs stay long; count what each job costs in screens and clicks as well. Model no; people none; weak. Cases: studio-go (own). Against: none found.
- **JOB-2** [stated] Turn a scripted walk of each job into a test with a committed baseline, so a change that adds screens or clicks fails before it merges. Model no; people checker; weak. Cases: studio-go (own). Against: none found.
- **JOB-3** [ours] Count each job twice, by its shortest route and as a newcomer walks it; the two differ, and an agent standing in for the newcomer takes fewer steps than people do. Model yes; people partly; medium. Cases: studio-go (own), UW walkthrough. Against: none found.
- **JOB-4** [stated] An audit read from code and screenshots can miss what walking the jobs finds: the screens and clicks each job needs, in what order, and whether pages agree; walk the jobs as well. Model partly; people model; weak. Cases: studio-go (own). Against: none found.
- **JOB-5** [stated] Count the jobs before the first change lands; a baseline taken afterwards cannot show what the change did to them. Model no; people none; weak. Cases: studio-go (own). Against: none found.
- **JOB-6** [stated] Agents told only to fold options keep them and add controls; say in the design what each job loses. Model partly; people checker; weak. Cases: studio-go (own). Against: none found.
- **JOB-7** [stated] A job walk that runs no scripts cannot see a control a script draws; draw the controls each job needs on the server, or the walk cannot count them. Model no; people checker; weak. Cases: studio-go (own). Against: none found.
